meta.date: ~600 BC (in vision, from the valley of Lemuel)

world_behind.title: The census formula of the covenant
world_behind.text: "As many as the sand of the sea" (v. 1) is Abraham's promise-language (Gen. 22:17), and its appearance over the promised land means the covenant took: the seed multiplied as sworn. The grief of the chapter is that the formula's first use here shows the multitudes "gathered together to battle, one against the other" (v. 2).

world_behind.title: A destruction that reads like fieldwork
world_behind.text: Sunk cities, burned cities, cities shaken to rubble; lightnings, tumbling mountains, broken plains. The catalog of verse 4 reads like seismic and volcanic devastation reported by a witness, and the fulfillment account (3 Ne. 8) will match it item for item.

world_behind.title: Twelve judging twelve
world_behind.text: Israel's court imagery ran on panels of judges, and the vision arranges its tribunals in ranks: the twelve apostles over the twelve tribes, the new world's twelve ministers under them (v. 9–10). The angel's structure is jurisdiction, not metaphor, and Mormon will still be teaching it at the record's end (Morm. 3:18–19).

world_behind.title: White garments were laundered
world_behind.text: Making cloth white was fuller's work: washing, beating, bleaching. The vision's image of garments "made white in his blood" (v. 10) borrows that labor and assigns it to the Lamb: purity in this record is cleaning, done by someone, at cost.

world_behind.title: Generations were how Israel measured mercy
world_behind.text: Blessing and consequence run "unto the third and fourth generation" in the law (Ex. 20:5–6), and the vision keeps that unit: three generations pass "in righteousness" (v. 11), and "many of the fourth" (v. 12); then the count runs out. To a hearer raised on the plates, the measure would likely have sounded both familiar and finite.

world_behind.title: Vision grief was a prophet's lot
world_behind.text: Seers before Nephi wept over what they were shown. Jeremiah wept over Jerusalem, and Daniel was sickened by his visions. This chapter puts Nephi in that company: the pattern of the promised land is shown to its first settler as a completed tragedy, and the record keeps his position fully visible: he is watching his own posterity lose.

words.text: The past tense of rend, to tear: "I saw the earth and the rocks, that they rent" (v. 4). Land described as cloth. It is the word the Gospels keep for the hour this vision is circling, when the veil of the temple and the rocks at Jerusalem rent as the Lamb died (Matt. 27:51), and it is the word the record will use when the fulfillment arrives on this side of the water, rocks "rent in twain" over the whole face of the land (3 Ne. 8:18).

spans.text: I saw the earth and the rocks, that they rent

words.text: The dream's mist has a physical cousin: "the vapor of darkness, that it passed from off the face of the earth" (v. 5). Where the symbolic mist never lifts in chapter 8, the literal one passes, and what its passing reveals is a sorted people: "multitudes who had not fallen" (v. 5). Weather ends; what it exposed remains.

cites.quote: the vapor of darkness, that it passed from off the face of the earth

spans.text: the vapor of darkness, that it passed from off the face of the earth

words.text: The Holy Ghost falls on the twelve ministers and they are "ordained of God, and chosen" (v. 7): office language inside a vision. Authority here is never self-assumed even in prophecy: the new world's ministry begins with a conferral, seen six centuries before it happens.

The mists lead men "away into broad roads" (v. 17), and the plural belongs to the picture: the path in the dream was one, strait and narrow, running along the rod (1 Ne. 8:20), while what the temptations offer is a whole network, wide and easy underfoot. The Lord draws the same contrast in his sermon, and the record will carry that sermon in its own pages, broad against strait, with destruction at the wide end (3 Ne. 14:13).

The divider between the building and the tree is named: "a great and a terrible gulf" (v. 18), and then defined, not as distance but as "the word of the justice of the Eternal God" (v. 18). The gap between pride and the tree is not geography; it is a standing judgment, and the record will reuse the image for the rest of its length.

words.text: The chapter's hardest word describes an endpoint, not a nature: it arrives only "after they had dwindled in unbelief" (v. 23), at the end of a mechanism the vision has just shown running (pride, temptations, war, forgetting). The same record insists that all are alike unto God (2 Ne. 26:33); this verse is where a people's chosen trajectory finally lands, and the record grieves it rather than gloats.

phrases.term: As the sand of the sea
phrases.text: The number promised to Abraham, fulfilled and immediately armed: the promised multitude appears mid-battle. The phrase carries the chapter's double vision (God keeps the numbers promise even while the numbered destroy each other) and quietly separates covenant blessing from covenant behavior.

The formula the Lord would later give for the last days (Matt. 24:6) appears here over the new world's whole timeline. Wars kill; rumors govern. The phrase names the dread between battles as part of the affliction, and the record's war chapters will bear it out.

phrases.term: He came down and showed himself unto them
phrases.text: The vision's summary of the volume's summit: after the darkness, the descent. The Lamb's new-world visit is foreseen here in one clause, and the record spends its central book (3 Ne. 11–28) unfolding what this sentence holds.

phrases.term: Made white in the blood of the Lamb
phrases.text: The paradox formula, whitening by blood, is shared exactly with John's Revelation (Rev. 7:14) and reused down the record (Alma 13:11). Purity in every canon that uses the image is a transaction: someone's garments, someone else's blood, and faith named as the point of exchange.

phrases.term: The depths thereof are the depths of hell
phrases.text: The river's key, withheld until now; and chapter 15 will add the unsettling note that Lehi never noticed the water's filthiness (1 Ne. 15:27). Some hazards are visible only from the mountain: the dream's happiest viewer stood beside depths he did not see.

The word from the Laban crisis (1 Ne. 4:13) returns as watched future: the angel shows the very dwindling that once justified a sword. From here the phrase becomes the record's standing diagnosis. Nations in this book rarely fall; they fade, by increments of forgetting.

verses.label: v. 7–10
verses.title: Three tiers of judges, stated as a chain
verses.text: The record does not simply name twelve ministers. It places them: the twelve apostles "shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel," the twelve ministers of Nephi's seed "shall be judged of them," and those ministers "shall judge thy seed." Three levels in two verses, with the reason for the middle link supplied, "for ye are of the house of Israel." The chain is the only place in these books where the relation between the two groups of twelve is spelled out, and it is put in the angel's mouth as an answer to a question, "Thou rememberest the twelve apostles of the Lamb?"

verses.label: v. 11–12
verses.title: A number introduced here and used four times afterward
verses.text: The record counts the righteous interval: "three generations pass away in righteousness," then "many of the fourth generation who passed away in righteousness." The same figure returns at 2 Nephi 26:9 in a prophecy and is walked off one generation at a time at 4 Nephi 1:14–22, with the failure arriving in the fourth. This chapter is the earliest statement of it. A number given in a vision six hundred years before the event, restated in a sermon, and then audited in a chronicle is a claim the record makes checkable against itself.

verses.label: v. 19
verses.title: A defeat with its cause assigned to the losing side
verses.text: The record does not report the outcome as a bare fact. It names two reasons in the same clause as the event: "because of the pride of my seed, and the temptations of the devil, I beheld that the seed of my brethren did overpower the people of my seed." One cause is internal and one external, and the internal one is listed first. The vision is being shown to the ancestor of the people who lose, and the explanation given to him puts the fault with them.

chapter.title: Prophecy as family grief
chapter.text: The vision turns from the Messiah to Nephi's own posterity, and the seer watches his line lose. The record never pretends otherwise afterward: its first author knew the ending before the beginning, and every hopeful sermon he writes later is written against this remembered silhouette.

chapter.title: Judgment before visitation
chapter.text: The chapter fixes the order the record's central event will keep: destruction, darkness, the lifting, then the descent (3 Ne. 8–11 runs the same sequence). The vision teaches readers how to hold the record's darkest chapters: as the hour before the showing.

chapter.title: The dream's map, completed
chapter.text: Tree, rod, and building were keyed in chapter 11; water, mist, gulf, and building's contents arrive here. Split across two chapters, the interpretation makes a quiet point: the dream's comforts and its hazards are learned separately, and a reader who stops at the loveliness of the tree has half a map.

chapter.title: Causes all the way down
chapter.text: The vision assigns causes at every turn rather than reporting outcomes alone. Verse 19 gives two, "because of the pride of my seed, and the temptations of the devil." Verse 22 gives one for the long decline, "these shall dwindle in unbelief." Verse 17 has already named the mist of darkness as "the temptations of the devil, which blindeth the eyes, and hardeneth the hearts." Three causal clauses in six verses, and each names a choice rather than a decree.

chapter.title: Purity is something done to you
chapter.text: The image appears twice in two verses and both times with the same cause attached: verse 10, "because of their faith in the Lamb of God their garments are made white in his blood," and verse 11, "These are made white in the blood of the Lamb, because of their faith in him." The whitening is stated as something done to the garments; they do not do it themselves. It is also dated: verse 11 counts "three generations" and verse 12 "many of the fourth," so the doctrine arrives attached to a population with a term.

chapter.title: The vision's hinge panel
chapter.text: Between the Messiah chapter (11) and the Gentile chapters (13–14), this panel carries the record's local story: the seed, the visit, the peace, the fall. The unit widens in circles: one Lamb, then one family's nations, then all nations. This chapter is the middle ring.

applications.title: Treat purity as laundry
applications.text: The garments are made white; nobody in the vision whitens their own. Take the image to the sacrament: bring the stained garment, name the faith, and let the exchange be his work, then live the week like someone wearing clean clothes he did not wash.

applications.title: Count your generations
applications.text: The vision's peace lasted as long as transmission did. Ask two questions: what of faith actually reached me from three generations back, and what am I doing, concretely, that could still be alive in my great-grandchildren?

applications.title: Audit the three mist-verbs
applications.text: The keyed temptations work in a sequence: blind the eyes, harden the heart, lead away. Run the audit on yourself in that order. What am I currently not seeing, where has repetition made me unfeeling, and where am I drifting on a broad road I never chose out loud?

applications.title: Name the gulf without flinching
applications.text: The divider between pride and the tree is the word of justice: real, fixed, and not yours to preach away. Where you have softened a true standard to keep peace, restate it kindly and plainly once, and let the kindness be in the tone while the standard stays whole.

applications.title: Write the two-part sentence about your own losses
applications.text: Nephi watches his seed overpowered, and the reason the vision gives has two halves: the pride of my seed, and the temptations of the devil. His own people are named first, and the adversary is not allowed to carry the whole explanation. When something of yours is overrun, write both clauses down: this is what came at us, and this is what we had already done that made it possible.

applications.title: Refuse the dwindle
applications.text: Nations in this record fade by forgetting. Choose one remembering practice (written answers to prayer, a weekly recital of a family deliverance, scripture at a fixed hour) and hold it precisely because nothing feels wrong yet.

questions.text: Which rumors of wars (news, feeds, forecasts) currently govern my peace more than my covenants do?
When the vapor around my life lifts, as it periodically does, what has the last darkness exposed about where I stand?
Do I actually treat purity as the Lamb's laundry, or as a reputation I maintain?
What reached me from the third and fourth generation back, and can I name what I am transmitting forward?
Of blinded eyes, hardened heart, and broad roads, which is my live danger this season?
Where in my discipleship am I dwindling, not deciding against anything, just remembering less?
